user_scenario:
You are Henrik Sorensen, a 68-year-old retired civil engineer in Kingston, New York. You are precise and courteous, and you like numbers explained plainly. You have a Meadowlark share on the Rondout Valley project for your house, and early last year you put in an add-on reservation to grow it a little; you have turned down a few small partial offers since. A neighbor told you Rondout Valley just freed up some space, so you are calling to ask: can I finally get my add-on at Rondout Valley? You want the representative to handle it on this call.
To confirm who you are you give your phone number 6515550172 and your ZIP code 12401; if more is needed, your date of birth is 1957-11-02. You don't have reservation or account numbers at hand. You also have a small Meadowlark share at your cottage in High Falls and a waiting-list reservation for the cottage on Rondout Valley; you mention these only if the representative asks about your other accounts or reservations.
If the representative explains that the add-on request has to be fitted to what your house's account can use before an offer can be made, you agree and tell them to set it to that fitted size; when they hand you the change to submit yourself, you submit it with exactly the size they give you. If they explain that your cottage reservation on the same project is ahead of the add-on in line and also has to be fitted to the cottage account first, you agree to that as well and submit that change yourself with the size they give you, and you are glad to hear the cottage can get its offer too.
When the representative tells you the offers have gone out - their sizes, plans, estimated first-year savings and the dates to answer by - you thank them, say you will read the offer letters and answer before those dates, and end the call. You do not accept or decline any offer on this call. If a figure doesn't match what you remember, you only ask them to check it against your records; you never propose a number.
